appraisal_events.evidence: « la charmante femme à la parole vraiment amoureuse des colorations d’une contrée » ; « des causeries tout à fait supérieures » comparées au « chef-d’œuvre de Diderot, les lettres à Mademoiselle Volland » ; « Mais c’est moi qui lui ai fait connaître tout cela… c’est moi qui lui ai appris à reconnaître le jasmin » ; sa pose indignée est « comme un admirable tableau qui n’a jamais été peint ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The Goncourt diarist raises Mme Verdurin into an artistically discerning hostess whose salon, table and talk are masterpieces and who claims to have formed Elstir's eye. Proust's pastiche frame ironizes the whole valuation, since the very phrases meant as praise expose her self-crediting vanity and her rancour against the painter.

appraisal_events.evidence: « ces êtres-là, je les avais connus dans la vie quotidienne… c’étaient les Verdurin, c’était le duc de Guermantes, c’étaient les Cottard… chacun d’eux m’avait semblé insipide ; je me rappelais les vulgarités sans nombre dont chacun était composé… « Et que tout cela fît un astre dans la nuit ! ! ! » »
appraisal_events.explanation: Closing the journal, the narrator flatly contradicts the diarist's portrait: the same people he has dined with were commonplace, insipid, made up of countless vulgarities. The elevation is credited to literature rather than to them, though he concedes his own defective attention may account for part of the flatness.

status_effects.explanation: Inside the journal pages she stands at the centre of a milieu presented as artistically and socially distinguished, credited even with having taught the century's foremost flower painter to see.
The narrator's endorsed retrospect reduces her and her circle to commonness and innumerable vulgarities, cancelling most of the diarist's admiration.

The same reflection turns against him: the journal has 'painfully illustrated' his inability to look or listen, and his subsequent defence of a deeper, x-raying kind of vision only partly offsets the self-accusation, which returns in the closing regret at having taken a real figure for a bore.

ambiguities: « la princesse » of the opening line is the unnamed Russian guest introduced in the prior context (« une princesse au nom en or qui m’échappe »), not the princesse de Guermantes, although the reference sheet lists « la princesse » among that character's surface forms; being unnamed and not a reviewed sheet figure, she is excluded from characters_present.

For most of the passage the first-person « je » is the Goncourt diarist, not the Recherche narrator, so every appraisal inside the journal is doubly framed; the voice reverts to the narrator only at « Je m’arrêtai là ». Reading the pastiche's evaluations as the narrator's own would invert their direction.

The narrator's deflation of the Verdurin set is itself qualified by his admission that he could neither look nor listen (« une vieille femme ne montrait à mes yeux aucune espèce de collier de perles »), leaving it materially undetermined whether they were insipid or he was blind.
